articles.title: Your Cloud Has Attack Paths No Scanner Can Find. Because They Don't Exist in Any Single Resource
articles.excerpt: ✓ Human-authored analysis; AI used for formatting and proofreading. Most cloud security tools work by checking individual resources against a library of known-bad patterns. Is this bucket public? Is t…
articles.body: ✓ Human-authored analysis; AI used for formatting and proofreading. Most cloud security tools work by checking individual resources against a library of known-bad patterns. Is this bucket public? Is this port open? Is this key unrotated? These checks are necessary. They're also insufficient. Because the most dangerous violations don't exist in any single resource. They exist in the RELATIONSHIPS between resources. They're detectable from the configuration structure alone, without any user input, without any tags, without any intent declarations.

articles.title: Encrypting personal data at rest in Symfony: a 60-line Doctrine type, and the four things it breaks
articles.excerpt: A review form asked me a yes/no question I could not answer with yes: do you encrypt personal data at rest and in transit? In transit, sure, TLS everywhere, that part is free in 2026. At rest, no. The…
articles.body: A review form asked me a yes/no question I could not answer with yes: do you encrypt personal data at rest and in transit? In transit, sure, TLS everywhere, that part is free in 2026. At rest, no. The app runs on a plain VPS with no full-disk encryption, and the database held customer names, addresses and email addresses in a json column, in clear, exactly as PostgreSQL received them. There are two ways out of that question. One is to click yes and move on, because everybody knows the reviewer will not ssh into your box. The other is to make the answer true. This post is the second one, taken from InvoicePilot , a Shopify app that issues invoices and therefore stores, by definition, the buyer's identity. The encryption itself is the easy part, and it is about sixty lines.

articles.title: Why AI Agents Are Replacing Traditional Software
articles.excerpt: A few years ago, building software meant writing a series of rules. If a user clicked a button, the application executed a function. If a condition was true, another function ran. Everything was predi…
articles.body: A few years ago, building software meant writing a series of rules. If a user clicked a button, the application executed a function. If a condition was true, another function ran. Everything was predictable because every possible outcome had already been programmed. That approach has worked for decades. But AI is changing the way software behaves. Instead of building applications that simply follow instructions, we’re beginning to build systems that can understand goals, make decisions, use tools, and adapt along the way. These systems are called AI agents, and I believe they’re one of the biggest shifts in software development since the rise of cloud computing. What exactly is an AI agent? An AI agent is more than a chatbot. A chatbot answers questions. An AI agent completes tasks.

articles.body: The term "grindhouse" used to refer to a particular style of movie theater that was once common in places like Hollywood Boulevard and Times Square. As far back as the 1920s, these theaters would adhere to a "grind policy" of showing low-budget movies at cut-rate ticket prices, often in a double or triple feature format. The theaters were usually located in the rough parts of a given city, which gave them a reputation: these were bad places that screened cheap, terrible films, which naturally gave them their own sort of charm.
